title: Postbiotics Formed during the Shelf Life of Probiotic Food Supplements Are Not Novel Foods: A Regulatory Case for Inactivated Lactic Acid Bacteria under Regulation (EU) 2015/2283
content: Postbiotics—preparations of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components—are expanding rapidly in the food supplement sector, yet their status under Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 remains unsettled, and operators are routinely told that inactivating a lactic acid bacterium (LAB) they already market creates a novel food. We test that proposition against the analytical and regulatory record. Published stability data show that a marketed probiotic supplement is never purely viable: about one third of cells are already dead at release, culturable counts then decline one to two orders of magnitude faster than total-cell counts, and residual fermentation medium carries secreted metabolites into the product from manufacture onwards. The inanimate fraction has therefore been consumed in the Union continuously and in quantity. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and Lactiplantibacillus pentosus have a documented pre-1997 history in European foods, are listed as not novel in the Commission’s Catalogue, and hold Qualified Presumption of Safety status that the European Food Safety Authority extends to non-viable biomass. Article 3(2)(a)(ii) contains no viability qualifier, and (vii) fails at its first limb because thermal treatment of fermented matrices predates 1997. Two determinations—heat-killed Propionibacterium freudenreichii (2021) and a heat-treated LAB fermentate (2026)—confirm this reading. Conventional thermal inactivation of LAB with pre-1997 history does not, by itself, create a novel food.
